status: Draft from the mishnah, R. Kulp and Kehati.

principles.t: A harmless ox (tam) pays only from its own body; the injured owner is either a new owner or a partner in it (Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon).
An ox can be an attested danger (mu'ad) for one kind of victim or one day, and harmless (tam) for others: full damages for the one, half for the other.
An Israelite's ox is exempt for damage to Temple property and to a gentile's ox; a gentile's ox pays full damages to an Israelite.
An ox that kills a person is stoned; the owner of an attested danger (mu'ad) pays ransom (kofer), the owner of a harmless one (tam) does not.
An ox is judged by its intention: it is exempt from death if it did not intend to kill a person.
A guard takes the owner's place; an owner who tied or locked his ox properly: the sages dispute, and the halakha follows Rabbi Judah.

terms.def: The payment an owner of an attested danger makes to ransom his life when his ox kills a person. It is the value of the person killed.
A person the court appoints to watch the ox of a deaf-mute, insane person or minor.
People to whom an ox is handed; they take the owner's place for its damage.

debates.title: What does the injured owner become?
debates.a: A creditor, paid first from the last victim backward.
debates.b: A partner in the ox, so the victims share.

debates.title: Is the ox harmless again when its owner recovers?
debates.b: It remains as it was. Rambam follows this view.

debates.title: A properly guarded ox that still damages
debates.a: Rabbi Meir: liable, harmless or not. Rabbi Judah: harmless, liable; attested danger, exempt from the full payment.
debates.b: Its only guarding is the knife. The halakha follows Rabbi Judah.
